item.title: America's Shipping Ports Now Face Thousands of Cyberattacks Each Day
item.description:
"A number of ports across the U.S. are reporting an onslaught of cyberattacks," reports The Hill, "amid a growing number of AI-enabled attacks targeting notable infrastructure." The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, which functions as the U.S.'s largest passage of oil exports, said it was targeted with "hundreds if not thousands" of attacks per day, according to reporting from the Financial Times. The port's chief executive, Kent Britton, told the outlet that attacks surged from "known bad actor" countries and organizations that are searching for high-profile targets. ["Experts link countries like Iran, North Korea and China to hacking operations targeting shipping infrastructure," the Financial Times reports.] The attacks against Corpus Christi's port went after its computer systems by attempting to find weaknesses. Attackers also sent phishing messages, posing as senior executives, to trick staff into allowing them access, per the Financial Times... "They're poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities," Britton said. "With AI, it'll only get more complicated." He stated the port was seeking additional help from Washington but "if you're playing defence, you have to get it right every time ... if you're planning offence, you only have to get it right once." The Port of Los Angeles — the country's busiest port — similarly stated that in August it had stopped 120 million attempted attacks into its networks through network exploitation, credential harvesting and malware attacks, Bloomberg reported. Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, expressed that all potential attackers "have to do is to get it right one time" and that it was "front of mind every day." "The attacks have escalated sharply in recent months..." reports the Financial Times, "exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing networks that enable international commerce." The FBI last week warned that hackers are using an AI tool named Artex to automate cyber attacks... The threat is growing across the US. The US Coast Guard reported a 17% increase in cyber maritime incidents last year and investigated cyber attacks on two US-bound oil tankers in August with the FBI... The agencies said the joint offshore security boardings on August 21 and 24 were to "ensure integrity of the vessel's operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised"... Ports are taking action to defend their waterways. The Port of Virginia, a major hub for consumer goods, agriculture and coal, said the threat of attacks is now "more acute because of the rise of AI". It is heavily investing in its cyber security team, with employees undergoing monthly training and drills with the US Coast Guard.... The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey is also investing heavily in cyber defence. A spokesperson said it has "multiple independent layers of protection" and "recovery plans with terminal operators and partners, so that critical operations can continue and cargo can keep moving". Other ports are reluctant to discuss the threat they face — and their defences. The Port of Oakland said it would not publicly discuss its "cyber security defences or protective measures", citing national security concerns. The article notes it's not just affecting U.S. ports. "Cybersecurity company Shieldworkz said Russia's Noname057(16) threatened European operators this October...

item.title: Have Investors Lost Their Faith in the AI Boom?
item.description:
"A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion," writes NPR, adding that "investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions." While the world embraced the AI boom ,"now many are having regrets," argues a Washington Post technology reporter: The AI boom's key ingredient has always been faith — that more money can be found to pay for it, that AI will keep rapidly improving, that the masses will come to love it, that business productivity and profits from AI are just around the corner. Faith is now in short supply... By mid-year, AI executives started to say that business customers were balking at the high prices charged by providers of cutting edge or "frontier" AI like Anthropic. Many businesses began to save money by hopscotching among a range of AI technologies, including low-priced options from Chinese companies... Investors began to rebel, too, against the trillions of dollars that AI companies are spending to construct data centers and provide them with computing equipment and electricity. Last month, Google's stock market value dropped by half a trillion dollars in a single day, when it seemed like even the rich technology leader would take longer than expected to see an AI financial payoff. Such stumbles by AI companies eroded faith in AI, said Howard Marks, an investor famous for predicting the dot-com bust. "It somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility," Marks told Bloomberg TV this month. Like many AI companies, Anthropic can't afford to cover its AI development costs. The company said it will keep coming back to investors for cash and needs a steady stream of customers to pay the $900 billion it owes in coming decades. Perhaps the biggest wild card for the AI boom is growing public resentment toward AI and data centers and widening fears of AI-enabled cyberattacks, human deaths and widespread job losses. In this month's midterm elections, Americans voted in a wave of elected officials who have been skeptical of the AI industry and construction of data centers. The results could slow the AI boom that's already hitting major bottlenecks, including difficulty lining up enough electricity to expand AI computer capacity... Diane Swonk, chief economist at the accounting firm KPMG, isn't surprised that the public is uneasy about AI. During the dot-com boom, she said that Americans' wages rose alongside corporate profits and U.S. inequality narrowed. By contrast the AI boom's economic and prosperity payoff has been uneven. "Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting," writes NPR, "just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000..."

item.title: Sellers are Closing Etsy Stores in Response to Its New AI Training Policy
item.description:
"I burned my Etsy shop to the ground this week," illustrator Aaron Millard posted on Instagram: 8 years, 11,200 sales, 3k+ reviews, hundreds in a customer base. Deleted. Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out (in Canada, anyways)... Etsy's new Terms of Use — going into effect December 15 — include this language in their section about "Your Content": You also recognize our legitimate interest in using it... This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy. "My work took years to learn and create," illustrator Millard wrote on Instagram. "I won't let it be stolen. It's not free fuel for an AI slop business model." Following Etsy's announcement "artists are shutting down their shops in droves," writes Cartoon Brew, "and posting illustrated goodbye notes to tell customers where to find them next." Ironically, just weeks ago, Etsy announced tighter rules on misleading AI product photos and bot-generated listings. The marketplace still allows sellers to list work generated from their own prompts, as long as they disclose the use of AI to buyers. Etsy says it uses sellers' content to spot fraud and help shoppers find products, and that it doesn't train models designed to copy artists' work. That said, the vague terms leave open just how its partners and vendors might use that same content... The artists posting their goodbyes have decided it's worth walking away from that revenue source to keep their work from being used to train AI. "In the wake of that reaction, Etsy vice president of customer operations James Ossman posted a separate update," writes PC Gamer, "saying it's not really like that at all... [T]hat 'we do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity.'" "... we're enabling actions like translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work," Ossman wrote. "We also use your content to develop tools that make running your shop easier, like listing optimization tools or stats summaries that help you better understand your shop's performance. As always, your needs and feedback help guide how we build and improve these tools." As for providing third-party access to that content, Ossman said that too is for "services and tools that can help you run your business," and promised that "when we partner with third parties, we do so thoughtfully to help protect your content and data." That hasn't satisfied everyone. Ossman's commitment doesn't exist within the actual terms of service, which as seen above states only that Etsy and partners can "use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." Ossman also noted in his update that the terms "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models," but that (as far as I can tell) applies to Etsy users and unauthorized third-parties, not Etsy itself or those it licenses... Others also complain that AI training should be opt-in rather than on by default — and worse, there's apparently no opt-out option available at all, so users who are opposed to having their work used for AI training for any reason are out of luck. Ironically, the blowup over Etsy's embrace of AI training comes just weeks after it earned plaudits for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, a move Ossman said was necessary to establish "trust" in the platform.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: The New 'Riemann Hypothesis' Proof Has Been Confirmed in Mathlib/Lean Communities
item.description:
"Experts say the claim checks out," reports the Guardian. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," reads Saturday's announcement on the Lean prover community blog: The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct... [Besides checking the code] The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean's official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean's logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit... We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof. "The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems," writes the Guardian, "even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems." "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Scientific American captured more mixed reactions Friday: As Massachusetts Institute of Technology mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "This is indeed an historic moment," Sutherland tells me today after he had independently compiled Alpöge's result in Lean. "The world has changed.... I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration." Sutherland says that it's worth celebrating the human work behind the development of Lean and LLMs — and, for that matter, the millennia of mathematical achievements upon which today's advance rests. But processing the earthshaking reality of what has occurred "is going to take some time." "There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof," he says. "And I can't wait to dig into them. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think."

item.title: Microsoft Admits Some Emails Bounced During Global Outlook Outage, Reveals New Failures
item.description:
After millions lost access to Microsoft 365 services (including Outlook) on November 12, Microsoft "has published the final post-incident report," writes Neowin, "and it reveals that some emails were never delivered to their intended recipients." "The report also details previously undisclosed failures affecting Microsoft's email security features..." Microsoft confirmed that all queued enterprise emails were eventually delivered and that it found no enterprise messages that were permanently lost. However, it is not the same with Outlook consumer users. The company acknowledged that some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days expired, and senders received non-delivery reports. Microsoft did not reveal how many emails were affected or how many users received non-delivery reports. The final report also reveals that the outage disrupted several important email security capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Office. For example, the Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) feature, which automatically removes malicious emails after delivery, was delayed because updated threat intelligence was unavailable. This means affected messages may not have been removed as quickly as usual. Microsoft also confirmed that users experienced problems opening URLs protected by Safe Links. Depending on their organization's security policies, some users may have encountered a "Skip verification" option when Safe Links attempted to check a URL... Microsoft also acknowledged that its first customer notification arrived approximately 20 minutes after the widespread impact began. It plans to improve automated outage notifications by the end of 2026 to improve communication. "Microsoft eventually restored the services about 12 hours later..."

item.title: Climate Change Talks Fall Apart In Final Hours Over Fossil Fuels
item.description:
NPR reports international climate talks "broke down in overtime hours, over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels." At Sunday's U.N. climate summit, "nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas." The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room... After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected — including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands. The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this." "Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions," the article notes, adding this is the first U.N. climate summit with a scientific consensus that the planet has already warmed past the threshhold countries agreed not to pass in 2015 of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit).

item.title: How Does GTA 6 Depict Electric Cars?
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto 6 as seen by the EV news site Electrek: GTA works as a mirror. In 2013, the EV was a punchline: a Tesla parody that overheated if you drove it too fast. In 2026, it's just another car in Vice City traffic, and the joke is on the guy in the pickup parked in the charging stall. That's a good sign of where EVs actually are. Satire goes after what's common, and Rockstar decided EVs are common enough to be part of everyday Leonida, more so in the city than in the Keys, just like real life. And that message is reaching a huge audience... Tens of millions of people are now driving EVs that charge as fast and as cheaply as gas cars, with no range anxiety. No automaker ad campaign gets close to that. They point out GTA 6 is "the first mainline GTA where energy matters." Gas cars burn fuel and need a pump, and EVs have a battery level and need a plug. Rockstar could have used that to make EVs a pain. It didn't. In my testing, the EVs have about the same range as the gas cars, charge just as fast as a fill-up, and cost the same or less to top up. Kotaku's range test backs that up. On the same highway loop, a Tesla Model 3 lookalike lasted 20 minutes and 23 seconds on a charge, longer than the Banshee sports car at 18 minutes and 31 seconds, and not far off an old pickup at 29 minutes and 8 seconds. Crossing the whole map by highway takes under 15 minutes, according to Kotaku. And finding a charger isn't a problem. Wccftech counted 120 EV chargers marked on the map, against just 57 gas stations... GTA has always been a parody of American life. With EVs, it's now slightly ahead of it. Florida is one of the strongest EV markets in the country, with a 9.4% share of new passenger vehicle sales in Q2 2026 versus 7.4% nationally, according to the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy.. But real Florida still has roughly three gas stations for every public charging location, based on the Alliance for Automotive Innovation's count of 3,267 charging locations and xMap's count of more than 10,500 gas stations. Leonida flips that ratio. GTA 6's Vice City has public fast chargers — branded "ReVolt America," which Electrek calls "an obvious copy of Electrify America's stations." And Electrek also spotted a giant charging hub at a power plant "with dozens of stalls and several EVs plugged in." There's even EV chargers being blocked by gas-powered cars, a phenomenon Electrek first covered in 2019

item.title: Python Devs Document 'De-fanging Dangerous Triggers In GitHub Actions'
item.description:
"A handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets," warn two security developers at the Python Software Foundation. Have dangerous triggers caused real incidents? Yes, repeatedly... The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one... When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one. pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway... Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises. The issue_comment trigger carries the same risk. This trigger fires when anyone comments on an issue or pull request, and the workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets... Sometimes the workflow pastes the comment text into a templated shell command, and the comment turns out to inject different instructions into the workflow shell. Python's official security developer in residence Seth Larson joined PyPI safety/security engineer Mike Fiedler to remove these dangerous trigger, also applying the policies Python Software Foundation-stewarded GitHub organizations (psf, python, and pypi). "They also wrote up technical documentation on how to roll these policies out to your own projects and organizations. "On a GitHub Team or Enterprise plan, you can turn them off for every repository in your organization with one policy. On a Free plan, you can do it one repository at a time. Set the policy up, check what it would block, then enforce it."

Its built-in solar panels are designed to add up to approximately 40 miles of driving a day from sunlight alone, under favorable conditions. "This is the moment our team has worked toward for years," said Chris Anthony, Co-CEO of Aptera. "To Accelerator #1, and to every reservation holder and shareholder who believed in this vehicle: thank you. We're working to complete more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible..." "What excites me about Aptera is how innovation can redefine the way we use energy in everyday mobility," said Martin Hartono, CEO of GDP Venture [and the proud recipient of Aptera solar car #1]. "By combining solar technology, battery power and an ultra-efficient vehicle design, Aptera offers a compelling solution for people who want to minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances. As an early believer in Aptera, I am proud to be part of this milestone and to see this vision become a reality." "Excuse me while I go find a hat to eat," jokes the blog InsideEVs... Nothing against Aptera specifically, but when a company hangs around for 20 years, while exchanging ownership hands several times without actually producing anything for customers, I start to get skeptical. However, Aptera Motors just did what so many doubters thought it'd never do: It delivered a road-legal production vehicle to one of its first early investors... [Aptera] does offer a interesting concept for customers who don't have long commutes and leave their car parked outside for most of the day while they work. In addition to plugging in to recharge, doesn't it sound nice to recoup your morning commute mileage with the sun while you're in the office? Whether this three-wheeled rolling solar panel ends up being a hit or not, and whether Aptera can stick around long enough to become a successful automaker, will take much longer to learn. But actually delivering a production car is a good place to start. Seven weeks ago Aptera said its first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, reports Electrek, with customer deliveries in early 2027 "subject to financing."

item.title: Quantum Computing's First Real-world Payoff May Come In Energy Solutions
item.description:
While quantum computing's biggest breakthroughs "are still likely to be years, if not decades, away," CNBC reports the technology is already being tested in energy applications, "from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production." Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture. Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently... For [quantum software company] Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator, the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The company says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing... [Phasecraft] is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones. Separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen. Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, [cofounder/CEO Ashley] Montanaro said the returns were there too. "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he said.

item.title: GTA 6: 32.5 Million copies, Cameos, and Easter Eggs - but No Physical Discs

(Though it makes for a very slow getaway, it's reportedly the GTA 6 vehicle that's least likely to crash...) - The jet-skiing dog in 'GTA 6' appears to be based on a real Florida dog. Swim too far out to sea in GTA 6 and a dog in goggles and a life jacket will come to the rescue on a jet ski... Florida locals quickly recognized it. The dog appears to be a nod to Loosy, a golden retriever from Fort Lauderdale who went viral in May riding a jet ski down the New River while her owner, Eddie Inch, towed her along on a jet-powered hoverboard... — GTA 6 isn't approved for sale in mainland China, but that hasn't stopped gamers from getting their hands on it — or Rockstar Games from promoting it there [Reuters reports]. The developer has been pushing the blockbuster game on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, despite the country's strict rules on violent video games. Meanwhile, Business Insider reports that Chinese gamers are circumventing the restrictions by using imported consoles and overseas digital stores. Zac Ling, a project manager at Shanghai-based consultancy Daxue Consulting, said gamers in mainland China could buy 3 million to 5 million copies of the game in its first week. The game's graphic content has also prompted censorship in Japan, according to IGN. - Beloved '80s song parody writer and GTA fan "Weird" Al Yankovic said Thursday that he's the host of the non-stop '80s radio channel Vice City FM in GTA 6. In social media posts, Yankovic said he also wrote some of the in-game commercials and voices the Burger Shot ads. Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News. Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels, according to the BBC. And "New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access." At its peak, nearly 8 million people were watching GTA 6 livestreams at the same time, Axios reported. PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing. [Around 75% of Grand Theft Auto VI sales have been on PlayStation 5, with the rest on Xbox, the BBC reported, citing estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower.] Yahoo news shares lots of crazy stories about GTA 6's world-building, like its cameos of real-world celebrities, its in-game hiking trails, and the way a GTA 6 house Rockstar first teased in 2021 hides a conspiracy-minded NPC who's convinced that he's in a video game. But they note that GTA 6 also brings questions on how videogames are sold and accessed: The game is being sold for $80 in boxes containing download codes instead of discs, meaning players can't trade in or resell their copies. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," [GameStop CEO Ryan] Cohen told Bloomberg. item.description:
San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet: Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral... ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.] Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day. But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle: Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle. It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane. "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror as they trap drivers in rapidly rising floodwater as monster storm hits California city." Waymos have sparked chaos in San Francisco as they trapped passengers in cars despite rapidly rising floods. Multiple self-driving vehicles were paralyzed across the streets and left those inside frantically calling the company to help get them to safety. One was trapped in the middle of a busy intersection when the car refused to go around an overflowing drain, leaving other drivers to go on the wrong side of the road to get around.... The San Francisco Chronicle also remembers that last year's power blackout caused 1,600 Waymo vehicles to stall "because they required a 'confirmation check' from a human operator before navigating stoplights after the power was cut. The alleged Russian agent was arrested in October for "stalking and harassing employees of the software and AI firm Palantir, sources told ABC News, because of its assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia." The agents also recovered three employee "target package profiles" that included their names, names of relatives, education and employment history, leadership qualities and a list of strengths and weaknesses. item.title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
item.description:
Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.) Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them... Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web's early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that's been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. "We're running on fumes," said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. "It keeps me up at night." Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing "more or less" ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the "new norm...." The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are "quite verbose," Ginn said. item.title: Earth has a New Moon
item.description:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN: Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

item.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED. "We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

item.title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
item.description:
A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins. The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester. "We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

item.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
item.description:
Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years. 2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof Add a new headline to the list... 2026: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order. [...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...] Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...] The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone." "If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind. In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system. But did a human beat the AI? The Washington Post reports: Just hours after AlpÃgeâ(TM)s claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors. But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag. âoeIf any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this,â he wrote. âoeWe are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.â

item.title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage. Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says. [...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. That court case remains ongoing. [...] According to the regulator, AT&T has proposed discontinuing the legacy telephone service in the state on or after June 1, 2027.

item.title: Trump Admin Still Won't Let TP-Link Sell Routers In US
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy."

item.title: I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again
item.description:
In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

The Forensic Approach to Deepfake Detection

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

Signaling a Video’s Provenance

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

Real-Time Verification

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today


Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

The rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers. The first launch isn't scheduled until early 2029, so we have a couple of years to see if this whole project even works. This is an experiment that Google calls a "long-term moonshot" to see if it's possible to put AI infrastructure in space by "tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit." The benefits of this would be massive. Data centers here on Earth are notorious hogs, with their snouts all over electricity grids, land and cooling systems. item.title: Amazon Fights the Delivery Protection Act With Homepage Banner, In-App Pop-Up
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill. When I log into Amazon today, I'm met with a vertical banner that reads: "ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order" with a button that says "Act now." The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn't specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I'm logged into Amazon. Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses. Clicking on "Act now" on Amazon's homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states: "Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The move marks an unusual expansion of Amazon's political advocacy, reports Ars, and raises concerns about the company's ability to influence shoppers and present a one-sided view of legislation. The bill, which also affects companies like FedEx and DoorDash, remains stalled in a City Council committee, with no vote scheduled.

item.title: Iowans Brace For Lead Dust Cloud As Army Plans to Detonate 5 Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals
item.description:

"The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory states. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure." PBS reports: Officials have released maps showing the potential drift north, and the Army will continue to update the maps based on weather. Some schools in the region have already canceled classes. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more could be affected. The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said. While the Army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough. [...] Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered. "The safety of our people and our neighbors is non-negotiable," Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production. The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November.

Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question.

item.title: Nvidia Approaches Arm Boss Rene Haas In Search For New CEO
item.description:
Nvidia has reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a replacement for co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid a personal scandal. According to Bloomberg, Haas is emerging as a leading contender for the job. The 64-year-old previously worked at Nvidia as general manager of its computing products business before joining Arm, giving him firsthand experience with the AI chip giant. The Guardian reports: Heidrick & Struggles, the recruiting firm hired by the company's board, has started contacting potential candidates, according to Bloomberg. It reported that Rene Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, is among those approached. [...] Haas, 64, is viewed as the leading contender for the top job at Nvidia, having previously worked at the $3.6tn company for seven years as the general manager of its computing products. Reports suggest that other potential candidates include: Ian Buck, an Nvidia vice-president; Lisa Su, AMD's chief executive; and Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer. Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Nvidia, Apple, Samsung and Qualcomm. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including more than 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech firm headquartered in Britain, now valued at $196bn. Haas told a tech conference in Austin on Wednesday that Huang was "a legend." "What he built at Nvidia is historic," he said. "You don't have many champions like that."

item.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard Disclose Cyberattack On Third-Party Vendors
item.description:
JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard have disclosed cyberattacks involving third-party service providers that exposed customer marketing data, including names, email addresses and, in some cases, phone numbers and postal codes. All three companies said their core systems or payment networks were unaffected, while JPMorgan emphasized that the incident was unrelated to the banking disruptions earlier this week. Reuters reports: A cyber extortion group called "n0n" claimed on November 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses," according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch. The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data. The same hacking group on November 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data. [...] The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses. The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. "Customers don't distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here," said Carissa Robb at SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm. "There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinizing the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared," Robb said.

item.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
item.description:
PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports: One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code. "An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell.
